metaDescription: Six cyclone dust separators compared by hose size, bin type, separation claims and fit, for shop vacuums and single-stage collectors.
expertTake: The Oneida Dust Deputy is the pick for anyone adding a pre-separator to an existing wet/dry vacuum on a budget, and the DEWALT 6 gallon rolling unit is the pick for a contractor who wants it ready to roll. Buyers who only sweep up occasional drywall dust do not need one at all.
introParagraphs: A cyclone separator is the cheapest filter you can buy, because it protects the filter you already own. Air enters tangentially, spins, and the heavier particles drop out by centrifugal force before the stream ever reaches the vacuum.

The idea is simple, so the differences are in the details: hose diameter, what the bin is, how the seal is made and how well the cone handles fine dust. This guide compares six that cover shop vacuums and small collectors.

products.name: Oneida Dust Deputy DIY Anti-Static Cyclone Separator
products.description:
The Dust Deputy DIY is a bare cyclone cone that you mount on your own bucket or drum. That is the reason it tops the list: you choose the bin size, so it grows from a 5 gallon bucket to a 30 gallon drum without a new purchase, and the cone itself is a proven design.

Its neutral vane technology is credited by the maker with raising efficiency by around 20 percent over earlier versions, and the anti-static material reduces the clinging dust and static shocks that plague plastic separators. The DIY label is accurate, because you must source a bucket, a lid and hoses, and the assembly takes an afternoon. Against the DEWALT rolling units it costs less but needs more of your time.

Ownership comes down to the seal. A leaky lid defeats the whole design, so use a gasketed lid and check it regularly. Empty the bin when it is half full to keep the cone from re-entraining dust, and check hoses for static clinging.
products.bestFor: A shop vacuum owner who wants a proven cyclone and is happy to build the bin.
pros: Proven cone design with neutral vane technology
Anti-static construction limits clinging dust
Mounts on whatever bin size you choose
Works for wet or dry debris
cons: Needs a bucket, lid and fittings you source yourself
Assembly takes some time and leaks if sealed poorly

products.name: DEWALT DXVCS002 6-Gallon Dust Separator for Wet/Dry Vacuums
products.description:
The DEWALT 6 gallon unit is a ready-built tank on a four-caster base, so it rolls around a job site and stays upright. It is aimed at capturing wood chips and general debris before they reach the vacuum, and it handles drywall and concrete dust too.

The maker claims up to 99.5 percent separation, which is a good number for a cyclone, though the real result depends on the vacuum airflow and the fine dust load. At 6 gallons it holds far less than the DEWALT 10 gallon stainless unit, but it weighs less and is easier to lift into a truck.

The four-caster base is the standout benefit, because it keeps the tank stable when you drag a hose across a floor. Empty it before it reaches the cone, wipe the lid gasket, and keep the hose connections tight so you do not lose suction.
products.bestFor: Contractors and garage users who want a rolling, ready-made separator.
pros: Four-caster base is stable and easy to move
Handles wood, drywall and concrete dust
Up to 99.5 percent separation claimed
Ready to use out of the box
cons: 6 gallon tank fills faster than larger models
Fine dust still reaches the vacuum filter in small amounts

products.name: DEWALT 10-Gallon Stainless Steel Tank Dust Separator
products.description:
This DEWALT separator has a 10 gallon stainless steel tank on casters, and it ships with a hose. A steel tank resists the dents, static and wear that plague plastic drums, and it handles sharp debris such as cut metal shavings or hard chips without scoring.

The 99.5 percent separation claim matches the 6 gallon unit, but the larger tank means longer between empties. The compromise is weight and bulk, since a full steel tank is heavy to lift. Compared with the Dust Deputy bucket build, it costs more but needs no assembly.

Steel does conduct static, so ground the hose if you use it for fine wood dust. Empty the tank before it is half full and keep the lid gasket clean so it seals tightly.
products.bestFor: A shop that wants a durable steel tank with long intervals between empties.
pros: Stainless steel tank resists dents and wear
10 gallons gives long intervals between empties
Rolls on casters
Ships with a hose
cons: Costs more than a bucket-based build

products.name: VEVOR 4-Inch Cyclone Separator with Metal Tank
products.description:
The VEVOR is the one built for 4 inch collector hose rather than small shop-vac hose. Its cone is a transparent ABS body, so you can watch the cyclone work, and it sits on a metal tank. Four inch connections matter because they are the standard on bag collectors, which this retrofit is meant to protect.

The maker claims a 99.61 percent separation rate, a bold number to compare against rivals that say 99.5 percent. Transparency is a real benefit, because you can see when the bin is filling and when debris is bridging in the cone. It is the cone for a single-stage collector, not for a wet/dry vac.

Check that your collector can handle the added restriction, because any cyclone adds pressure drop. Seal the joints with proper tape or gaskets, and ground the cone if you run a lot of dry fine dust.
products.bestFor: An owner of a single-stage collector who wants a pre-separator in front of a 4 inch hose.
pros: Sized for 4 inch collector hose
Clear cone shows how the cyclone is working
Metal tank for durability
Claims 99.61 percent separation
cons: Adds restriction to a modest-powered collector
Not designed for small shop-vac hoses

products.name: Mullet Cyclone Separator with Cut-to-Fit PVC Connection
products.description:
The Mullet is a one-piece parabolic cyclone with a rigid PVC connection that you cut to fit your bucket. The point of the PVC tube is to eliminate the bolts, bungees and duct tape that make homemade bucket setups fragile.

The parabolic one-piece body has no seams to leak, which is the cause of most lost performance in bolted designs. It claims to remove over 99 percent of debris before the vacuum. The cut-to-fit tube makes it adaptable, but it also demands a decent saw cut, since a ragged tube leaks.

Use a clean, flat-topped bucket and a gasketed lid. Cut the PVC carefully so the cone sits level, and check the joints after the first few uses as vibration finds weaknesses.
products.bestFor: A tinkerer who wants a seamless cone and a rigid connection on a custom bucket.
pros: Seamless one-piece body has few leak points
Rigid PVC connection replaces tape and bungees
Claims over 99 percent pre-separation
Adapts to buckets of various heights
cons: You still provide the bucket and lid

products.name: Cikawit Low-Profile Separator for 5-Gallon Buckets, 90-Degree Elbows
products.description:
The Cikawit is a low-profile lid that turns a standard 5 gallon bucket into a cyclone separator with 2.5 inch hose connections. The low profile keeps the setup compact, so the bucket does not tower over the vacuum.

Elbows come in the kit, which saves a trip to the hardware store, and the whole thing is designed to drop onto a bucket you already own. The capacity is limited to 5 gallons, so heavy chip loads fill it quickly. Compared with the Dust Deputy, it is a ready-made lid rather than a bare cone.

Seal the lid and keep the bucket square. Empty it at about half full. Light shop cleanup suits it, while a planer would overwhelm it.
products.bestFor: A shop vacuum user who wants a compact bucket-lid separator with minimal fuss.
pros: Fits any standard 5 gallon bucket
Low profile keeps the setup compact
Includes 90 degree elbows
2.5 inch hose fits common vacuum hoses
cons: 5 gallon bucket fills fast with chips
Plastic lid flexes under heavy suction

buyingCriteria.explanation: A cyclone has to match the hose and the vacuum. The Cikawit and the Dust Deputy suit 2.5 inch shop-vac hoses, while the VEVOR is sized for 4 inch collector hose. Using a reducer restricts airflow and defeats the purpose of the separator. Check your vacuum or collector port before buying.

The bin decides how often you empty. The DEWALT 10 gallon steel tank outlasts the 6 gallon version, and the 5 gallon bucket lids fill fastest. A bare cone like the Dust Deputy lets you scale from a bucket to a drum. Remember that a full bin loses efficiency as dust re-enters the cone.

A cyclone works only if the bin is airtight, because a leak at the lid pulls air straight past the cone. The Mullet one-piece body removes a leak point, and gasketed lids matter on all of them. If you hear a whistle, there is a leak. Test with a hand over the inlet, and fix anything that rattles.

Plastic cones build static, which makes fine dust cling and gives a nasty shock. The Dust Deputy uses an anti-static material, and a steel tank like the DEWALT 10 gallon conducts static away if grounded. In a dry winter shop, static is a real nuisance and a reason to choose carefully.

Claims of 99.5 percent or 99.61 percent separation apply to particles above a certain size. The finest dust, below a few microns, still reaches the vacuum filter. A cyclone extends filter life, but it does not replace a good filter. Treat the claim as a comparison point, not a guarantee. Makers rarely say which particle size the percentage refers to, so two separators quoting 99.5 and 99.61 percent cannot be ranked against each other with any confidence. Judge them by seal quality, bin size and how well the hose fits instead.

A rolling tank like the DEWALT units follows you across a floor and stays upright. A bucket lid like the Cikawit or Dust Deputy sits on the floor with a short hose. Rolling units cost more but avoid the tipping and hose tangle that bucket setups create.

specDecoder.watchFor: The DEWALT units say 99.5 percent and the VEVOR 99.61 percent, which are too close to call.

specDecoder.meaning: The diameter of the inlet and outlet. A mismatch forces reducers that restrict airflow.
specDecoder.watchFor: The VEVOR fits 4 inch hose and the Cikawit 2.5 inch.

specDecoder.meaning: How much debris the bin holds before dust re-enters the cone.
specDecoder.watchFor: The DEWALT 10 gallon tank doubles the 5 gallon bucket lids.

specDecoder.meaning: A material or design that reduces static buildup and clinging dust.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Dust Deputy DIY is the one marketed as anti-static.

specDecoder.watchFor: The Cikawit is built around this; the rolling DEWALT tanks are taller.

howWeEvaluated.title: Separation design
howWeEvaluated.description: We read each maker's stated separation rate and the cone construction. A seamless one-piece cone like the Mullet and a proven neutral vane design like the Dust Deputy earn credit. Claims near 99.5 percent were treated as equal.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fit and hose size
howWeEvaluated.description: We matched each model to the hose it is built for. The VEVOR at 4 inches suits collectors, and the Cikawit at 2.5 inches suits shop vacs.

howWeEvaluated.title: Bin capacity and durability
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared tank sizes and materials. The DEWALT 10 gallon steel tank leads, while 5 gallon bucket lids sit at the low end.

howWeEvaluated.title: Setup effort
howWeEvaluated.description: Ready-made rolling units rank above DIY builds for convenience. The Dust Deputy DIY and the Mullet require you to source and cut parts.

howWeEvaluated.title: Static and leak resistance
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered anti-static materials, seals and the number of joints. Fewer joints and grounded steel rank higher.

cards.label: DIY bucket
cards.text: The Dust Deputy, Mullet and Cikawit turn a bucket into a separator. They are cheap and flexible, but you supply the bin and make sure it seals.

cards.label: Ready-made tank
cards.text: The DEWALT 6 and 10 gallon units arrive complete with casters and a lid. They cost more and weigh more, and they save an afternoon of building.

howToChoose.note: Handy owners pick a DIY cone; contractors pick the DEWALT tanks. The cone itself is the same physics either way, so the decision is really about whether an afternoon of cutting, drilling and sealing is something you enjoy or something you would rather pay to avoid. If you already own a spare bucket and a hole saw, the Dust Deputy route is hard to beat on cost per year of service.

howToChoose.subheading: For Protecting a Shop Vacuum Specifically

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Look for a cone that matches your hose, a bin that seals, and enough volume that you are not emptying every few minutes. Avoid anything that forces a reducer.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Dust Deputy DIY is the best balance of cost and proven design, and the DEWALT 6 gallon is the best ready-made choice.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Spend more if you vacuum heavy chips or work on job sites; the DEWALT 10 gallon steel tank is the durable choice. Also spend more to avoid assembly with a rolling unit.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Save if you do light cleanup. A Cikawit lid on a bucket you already own does the job. The same applies if you only run a vacuum after a project rather than during one, because an hour of fine dust a month will not justify a steel tank on wheels. Put the difference toward a better vacuum filter instead, since that is where fine dust is finally stopped.

maintenance.why: A full bin lets dust re-enter the cone and reach the vacuum filter.
Fine dust coats the cone walls and slows the spin. Wipe it with a dry cloth, and look for a ring of packed dust near the outlet, which is the first sign that the bin was left too full for too long.
A leaky lid pulls air past the cone. Replace a worn gasket.
Cracked hoses and loose clamps cost suction. Replace damaged sections.
Static clings dust to plastic. A grounding wire or anti-static spray reduces it.

faq.q: Does a cyclone separator replace a filter?
faq.a: No. It pulls most debris out before the filter, which extends filter life. The finest dust still reaches the filter, so keep it clean.

Slightly, because any cyclone adds restriction. A good one costs little, and a full bin costs far more. Empty it regularly. Most of the suction complaints we see in owner feedback trace back to a flattened hose, a leaking lid or a clogged vacuum filter rather than the cone itself, so check those three before blaming the separator.
Five gallons suits light cleanup, and a larger drum suits heavy chips. The Dust Deputy cone fits larger bins, while the lid kits are built for 5 gallon buckets.

faq.q: Can I use one with wet debris?
faq.a: The Dust Deputy and DEWALT units are marketed for wet or dry debris with a wet/dry vacuum. Check the manual, and empty and dry the bin afterwards.
It lets you watch the cyclone work, which helps with diagnosing clogs. Clear plastic builds more static, so ground it.

faq.q: Do I need one with a dust collector?
faq.a: A separator in front of a single-stage collector keeps the bag clean longer. A 4 inch unit like the VEVOR is built for that job. The catch is airflow: a small 1 HP collector has little pressure to spare, so add the cyclone only if the machine still pulls well with a clean bag, and keep the duct between collector and cone short and smooth.
